value.overview: The Lesser Kiskadee (Philohydor lictor) is a small, water-associated tyrant flycatcher of tropical Central and South America. It is often seen near quiet rivers, ponds, marshes, lagoons, and mangroves, where it perches above the water and captures insects. Its yellow underparts, dark eye mask, white throat, and olive-brown upperparts distinguish it from the larger Great Kiskadee. In Costa Rica, it is considered a very rare or accidental species rather than a regular, widespread resident.
value.classification: The Lesser Kiskadee belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae. It is the only species in the genus Philohydor, although it was formerly placed in the genus Pitangus.
value.identification: A small, compact kiskadee with olive-brown upperparts, a grayish crown, a conspicuous black mask through the eye, and a white throat. The underparts are bright yellow, sometimes with an olive wash on the breast. The bill is relatively short and broad compared with that of the Great Kiskadee. Its wings and tail are dark, and pale wing edges may be visible at close range. Identification should be careful in Costa Rica because similar yellow-bellied flycatchers occur there.
value.rangeHabitat: The Lesser Kiskadee is distributed mainly from Nicaragua and Trinidad south through northern and eastern South America to parts of Bolivia, Paraguay, and southern Brazil. It favors densely vegetated margins of slow-moving streams, oxbow lakes, ponds, marshes, flooded forest, lagoons, and mangrove channels. In Costa Rica, it is recorded only very rarely or as an accidental visitor, with no well-established regular distribution. Any Costa Rican sighting should be documented carefully with photographs or sound recordings.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident within its tropical range, with local movements possible in response to water levels or food availability. In Costa Rica it is a rare or accidental species, not a regular migrant.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs during the local rainy or early wet season in different parts of its range. The species usually nests close to water, using cavities, holes, or protected sites in trees and vegetation. The nest is typically bulky and constructed from plant fibers and other soft material. Both adults participate in territorial defense and care of the young. Details of its breeding biology are better documented in South America than in Costa Rica, where the species is not known to breed regularly.
value.dietFeeding: The Lesser Kiskadee feeds mainly on insects and other small arthropods captured by short flights from exposed perches. It may also take small fish, aquatic organisms, fruits, and other small prey when available. It commonly hunts along shaded water margins, watching from branches or reeds and dropping toward the surface or nearby vegetation. Its close association with quiet freshwater and wetland habitats is a useful clue to identification.
value.behavior: Usually solitary or found in pairs, the Lesser Kiskadee is an alert, active perch-and-sally feeder. It often sits quietly near water before making a quick flight to seize prey, then returns to a favored perch. It may defend a small territory around a pond, stream edge, or marsh. Calls are sharp and varied, and the species can be conspicuous when calling despite spending much of its time among dense waterside vegetation.

conservation.populationTrend: No major global conservation decline is established strongly enough to change its Least Concern assessment. Local populations may be affected by changes to wetlands and waterways.
